definition: A space constructed by iteratively attaching cells (disks) of increasing dimension to a base space
A cell complex satisfying two additional conditions: closure-finiteness (C) and weak topology (W). Each closed cell meets only finitely many other cells
A continuous deformation of one map into another. Two maps f,g: X→Y are homotopic if there exists a continuous F: X×[0,1]→Y with F(x,0)=f(x) and F(x,1)=g(x)
A map f: X→Y such that there exists g: Y→X with gf ≃ id_X and fg ≃ id_Y. X and Y are then homotopy equivalent
A subspace A⊂X such that there exists a retraction r: X→A with the inclusion i: A→X satisfying ir ≃ id_X. The subspace captures the homotopy type of the whole space
A space that is homotopy equivalent to a point. Equivalently, the identity map is homotopic to a constant map
π₁(X,x₀): the group of homotopy classes of loops based at x₀ in X, with concatenation as group operation
A path-connected space X with trivial fundamental group π₁(X)=0. Every loop can be continuously contracted to a point
A space X̃ with a map p: X̃→X such that each point of X has a neighborhood U evenly covered by p (p⁻¹(U) is a disjoint union of open sets each mapped homeomorphically to U)
If X = U₁∪U₂ with U₁,U₂,U₁∩U₂ path-connected, then π₁(X) is the amalgamated free product π₁(U₁)*_{π₁(U₁∩U₂)} π₁(U₂)
A group with a set of generators and no relations other than the group axioms. The fundamental group of a wedge of circles is free
A homeomorphism f: X̃→X̃ of a covering space that commutes with the projection p. The group of deck transformations acts on fibers
A simply connected covering space. It exists for any path-connected, locally path-connected, semi-locally simply connected space
Homology defined for simplicial complexes using chains of oriented simplices, boundary maps, and the quotient Hₙ = ker∂ₙ/im∂ₙ₊₁
Homology defined for any space using continuous maps σ: Δⁿ→X (singular simplices). More general than simplicial homology but agrees on simplicial complexes
A sequence of abelian groups ···→Cₙ₊₁→Cₙ→Cₙ₋₁→··· connected by boundary maps ∂ with ∂²=0
The homomorphism ∂ₙ: Cₙ→Cₙ₋₁ in a chain complex. For singular homology, ∂σ = Σᵢ(-1)ⁱσ|[v₀,...,v̂ᵢ,...,vₙ]
An n-chain z with ∂z=0. The group of n-cycles is Zₙ = ker∂ₙ
An n-chain b that equals ∂c for some (n+1)-chain c. The group of n-boundaries is Bₙ = im∂ₙ₊₁
Hₙ(X) = Zₙ/Bₙ = ker∂ₙ/im∂ₙ₊₁. Measures n-dimensional holes in X. H₀ counts connected components, H₁ counts independent loops
βₙ = rank(Hₙ(X)). β₀ = number of connected components, β₁ = number of independent loops (first Betti number)
χ(X) = Σₙ(-1)ⁿβₙ = Σₙ(-1)ⁿrank(Hₙ). For a CW complex, also equals Σₙ(-1)ⁿcₙ where cₙ is the number of n-cells
A sequence of homomorphisms ···→A→B→C→··· where the image of each map equals the kernel of the next
An exact sequence 0→A→B→C→0, meaning A injects into B and C is the quotient B/A

term: long exact sequence of a pair
definition: ···→Hₙ(A)→Hₙ(X)→Hₙ(X,A)→Hₙ₋₁(A)→··· relating the homology of a space, a subspace, and the relative homology
Hₙ(X,A) = Hₙ(C*(X)/C*(A)). Measures holes in X that are not already in A
For X = A∪B: ···→Hₙ(A∩B)→Hₙ(A)⊕Hₙ(B)→Hₙ(X)→Hₙ₋₁(A∩B)→··· A computational tool for homology
If Z⊂A⊂X with closure(Z)⊂interior(A), then Hₙ(X,A)≅Hₙ(X\Z, A\Z). Allows cutting out subsets without changing relative homology
For f: Sⁿ→Sⁿ, the integer d such that f*: Hₙ(Sⁿ)→Hₙ(Sⁿ) is multiplication by d
Homology computed using the CW structure. The cellular chain group Cₙ is free abelian with one generator per n-cell. Often the most efficient computation method
H̃ₙ(X): modified homology where H̃₀ is the kernel of the augmentation map ε: C₀→Z. For non-empty connected X, H̃₀=0 while H₀=Z
SX = X×[0,1]/(X×{0}, X×{1}). Suspension shifts homology: H̃ₙ(SX)≅H̃ₙ₋₁(X)
X∨Y: the union of X and Y with a single point identified. π₁(S¹∨S¹) is the free group on two generators
Cf = Y ∪_f CX for a map f: X→Y. Used to construct spaces with prescribed homology
Mf = (X×[0,1] ⊔ Y)/(x,1)~f(x). Deformation retracts onto Y and contains X as a subspace
A continuous map r: X→A where A⊂X and r|_A = id_A. If it exists, A is called a retract of X
A continuous map f: X→Y induces homomorphisms f*: Hₙ(X)→Hₙ(Y) and f*: π₁(X)→π₁(Y) that are functorial: (gf)* = g*f*
If f≃g: X→Y then f*=g*: Hₙ(X)→Hₙ(Y). Homology depends only on the homotopy type, not the specific space
Homology can be computed with coefficients in any abelian group G: Hₙ(X;G). Common choices: Z, Z/2, Q, R
A collection of simplices closed under taking faces and intersections. A combinatorial structure for building topological spaces
The n-simplex Δⁿ is the convex hull of n+1 affinely independent points. Δ⁰=point, Δ¹=segment, Δ²=triangle, Δ³=tetrahedron
A continuous map γ: [0,1]→X. A loop is a path with γ(0)=γ(1). Path-connectedness means any two points can be joined by a path
X/~ for an equivalence relation ~. Points identified by ~ become a single point. The quotient topology is the finest making the projection continuous
A continuous map φ: Sⁿ⁻¹→X used to attach an n-cell eⁿ to X, forming X ∪_φ Dⁿ. The building block of CW complex construction
Xⁿ: the union of all cells of dimension ≤n in a CW complex. X⁰⊂X¹⊂X²⊂··· is the skeletal filtration
Elements of finite order in a homology group. Torsion in H₁ detects non-orientability (e.g., H₁(RP²)≅Z/2)
